description: The Delhi Sultanate refers to the period in Indian history from 1206 AD to 1526 AD. During this era, five major Islamic dynasties ruled over large parts of the Indian subcontinent: the Mamluk (Slave), Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, and Lodi dynasties.

sections.title: Mamluk or Slave Dynasty
sections.description: The first dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, founded by Qutbuddin Aibak in 1206 AD. It is also known as the Ilbari or Mamluk Dynasty.

key_concepts.explanation: An administrative system introduced by Iltutmish where state officials and soldiers were granted land revenues (Iqta) in lieu of cash salaries.
A powerful council of 40 loyal Turkic nobles created by Iltutmish to help him administer the empire. It was later destroyed by Balban to assert absolute royal power.

historical_events.significance: Established the dynasty with Lahore as his capital. He was famously known as 'Lakh Bakhsh' (Giver of Lakhs) due to his immense generosity.
She was the daughter of Iltutmish and holds the distinction of being the first and only female Muslim ruler of medieval India.

important_facts.fact: Ghiyasuddin Balban adopted the rigid 'Policy of Blood and Iron' to ruthlessly suppress rebellions and internal threats.
Balban introduced the Persian festival 'Navroz' in India, along with the strict court rituals of 'Sijda' (prostration) and 'Paibos' (kissing the Sultan's feet).

sections.title: Khalji Dynasty
sections.description: Founded by Jalaluddin Firoz Khalji, it was the shortest-ruling dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate (1290-1320 AD) but witnessed massive territorial expansion.

key_concepts.explanation: A strict economic regulation implemented by Alauddin Khalji to fix the prices of all essential commodities, ensuring a large standing army could be maintained on lower salaries.
Military reforms by Alauddin Khalji involving the branding of horses (Dagh) and maintaining a descriptive roll of soldiers (Huliya) to prevent corruption and proxy substitutions.

historical_events.significance: He maintained the first permanent standing army of the Sultanate and launched highly successful campaigns into South India led by his general, Malik Kafur.

key_associations.extra_info: Known as 'Tuti-e-Hind' (Parrot of India). He is credited with the invention of the Sitar and Tabla, and is considered the father of Qawwali.

sections.title: Tughlaq Dynasty
sections.description: Founded by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq in 1320 AD. It was the longest-ruling dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate (1320-1414 AD), known for its ambitious but often flawed administrative experiments.

historical_events.significance: Muhammad bin Tughlaq ordered the shift of his capital from Delhi to Devagiri (renamed Daulatabad) to better control the Deccan, a move that ended in disastrous failure.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced copper and brass coins at par with the value of silver coins. It failed massively due to widespread forgery.

important_facts.fact: The famous Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta visited India during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq and documented his experiences in his book 'Rihla'.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq was the first Sultan to impose the Jizya tax separately on the Brahmins.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq is credited with establishing the largest network of irrigation canals in medieval India and founding cities like Hisar, Firozabad, and Jaunpur.

sections.title: Sayyid and Lodi Dynasties
sections.description: The Sayyid dynasty (1414-1451 AD) was founded by Khizr Khan. The Lodi dynasty (1451-1526 AD), founded by Bahlol Lodi, marked the first Afghan empire in India.

historical_events.significance: Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra to control the Rajputana region and subsequently made it his capital.
Babur decisively defeated Ibrahim Lodi. This battle marked the definitive end of the Delhi Sultanate and the beginning of the Mughal Empire in India.

important_facts.fact: Sikandar Lodi was a patron of literature and composed Persian poetry under the pen name 'Gulrukhi'.
Ibrahim Lodi holds the unique distinction of being the only Sultan of Delhi to be killed on the battlefield.

sections.title: Administration, Departments and Architecture
sections.description: The administrative framework of the Delhi Sultanate was highly centralized. It also saw the fusion of Islamic and Indian architectural styles, leading to the Indo-Islamic architecture.

key_concepts.explanation: The Ministry of Military Affairs, established by Balban. The head of this department was known as the Ariz-i-Mumalik.
The Department of Revenue Arrears, set up by Alauddin Khalji to inquire into revenue collections and extract pending dues from officers.
A separate Department of Agriculture created by Muhammad bin Tughlaq to bring uncultivated land under the plow and provide state loans (Taccavi) to farmers.

key_associations.extra_info: Located in Delhi. Aibak started its construction, and Iltutmish completed it. It was dedicated to the famous Sufi saint Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki.
The magnificent southern gateway to the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque within the Qutb Complex, marking the first use of true arches and domes in India.
An extensive Arabic text written by Al Biruni, who accompanied Mahmud of Ghazni, detailing the religion, philosophy, and society of India.
